name: Bell Push
tagline: Momentary by design: it conducts only while you hold it, which is why the bell rings once and stops.
terminals: Two terminals on a simple bell push — one conductor in, one out
Some illuminated pushes need a neutral as well
parts: Button cap — the part you press
Bezel or surround — the decorative ring and plate
Spring return — drives the contacts open again
Normally-open contacts — closed only while pressed
Fixing screws or a hidden clip
safety: Most bell circuits run at extra-low voltage from a transformer or a bell unit, which makes the wiring itself safe to handle. The transformer does not: it is mains equipment, mounted in a cupboard or the consumer unit, and it must be isolated before any work on it.

points.label: Button
points.detail: The cap you press. It pushes a plunger onto a spring contact, and the spring is what makes the action momentary — release it and the circuit opens again however long you hold it.

points.label: Bezel / surround
points.detail: The ring and plate that make the push weatherproof and tidy. Outdoor pushes carry an IP rating; a push that lets water into the back of the mechanism will corrode the contacts long before it fails electrically.

points.label: Surround plate
points.detail: Mounts on a back box or directly to the frame. Illuminated pushes need a neutral at the plate, which older bell wiring often does not provide.

points.label: Fixing screws
points.detail: Visible screws, or a clip-on cover that hides them. Screwing a push to a damp frame without a gasket lets water track straight into the terminals.

points.label: Rear contacts (normally open)
points.detail: The contacts are open at rest and close only while the button is held. That is the whole point of a bell push: hold it down and the bell keeps ringing, let go and it stops — no latching, no second press.
